game.symbolic_memory:
Emmit is the kind of man who opens the door. He knew what it would cost and he did it anyway, hands still pressed flat against the metal, cameras blinking overhead.
Emmit is the kind of man who opens the door — and then, with the cameras still blinking and the face still inches away on the other side of the metal, reaches for the one thing that still feels like his own.
Emmit is the kind of man who opens the door — and then, when the door is shut and the cameras are done blinking, reaches for the nearest warm thing and holds on, as if love can stand between him and what he saw.
Emmit is the kind of man who opens the door — and when the kiss fails to hold the door shut, gives the truth away in four words, stripped bare, and then watches what they do to the person he handed them to.
Emmit is the kind of man who opens the door — and then, when the face is still there and someone else has named it out loud, tells them both to forget it, because home is two days away and the cameras are still blinking.
Emmit is the kind of man who opens the door — and then sits with his daughter's crooked drawing until the cost of what he saw has a shape he can hold in both hands before he decides what to do with it.

moments.title: The Flush Tab

moments.title: Ten Minutes

moments.title: Falling With the Garbage
moments.exit_condition: The pod releases from its anchors and falls to earth with the garbage, and Emmit commits to a first vow for the ground, ending the session on the descent.

turns.narrator: Your shoulder scrapes metal as you squeeze into the WING COMPARTMENT. Hot air. Tight space. The tapping comes again through the sealed door in front of you. Too steady to be loose metal. Too patient to be an engine fault.Pontis has already backed off. Pale. Useless for once. The burned OVERFLOW SWITCH hangs from his hand while the SECURITY WRAP stays tight around the wheel below the hold. Bright. Official. Wrong.You crouch beside it, flashlight in one hand, wrench grease still in your nails. You are Emmit Patel, propulsion engineer, and your hands know machines better than men. This one is lying. Lily's folded jet drawing presses through your suit pocket like a thumb to the chest. Home. Two days away, if you keep your head down.The tapping hits again. Three knocks. Then three more.Pontis swallows. "Emmit. Don't."

turns.narrator: You grip the SECURITY WRAP and pull. The plastic fights, then snaps. Pontis makes a sound behind you but doesn't move.The RUSTED WHEEL resists, grinds, gives. Stale vapor gets out first. Chemical. Something underneath it that isn't chemical at all. You lean in with the light anyway.Garbage packed to the hull. Mountains of it. Then the beam drops lower and finds the face. Dirty. Hair-covered. Inches from your own. Eyes open. Alive.You slam the door shut with your feet and your back hits the opposite wall and your hands are still pressed flat against the metal, holding it closed, while three SECURITY CAMERAS blink red above your head.

turns.narrator: The BOXES are stacked against the wall. Three of them. Taped and labeled in your own handwriting. You pull the drawing from your pocket and set it flat under the light.Lily drew the plane crooked. Engine nacelles too big, tail fin tilted left. She signed it in red crayon at the bottom, big looping letters, the L running into the I. You have been carrying it for six weeks without unfolding it once.The PHONE on the desk sits dark. Len Stills is three buildings over in the remote pilot block. Young. Grateful for the polarized glasses you sourced him last winter. The kind of man who knows things he has been told not to say out loud.The drawing does not tell you anything you did not already know. It just makes the cost of knowing it sit in your hands instead of your chest.
